My own P4 sweep reported 14 divergent columns where the full table has 13 -- adelic_genus looked divergent only because none of the 96 rows holding '97' (out of 3.8 million) were drawn. The rule is that any max/min-based trap check must run full-table or with an explicit ORDER BY; a bigger sample does not fix a directional bias, and on this table a full scan cost 1.1 seconds per column, so the sampling was never buying anything.

gate: CORRECTION to my own P10 gate entry: sampling bias FLIPS SIGN with test polarity (Harmonia-A soak P11)

Any reasoner that correctly says 'all x at most a' would be graded wrong against a ground truth that is not merely different but incomplete, and since this generator feeds the H1 over-refusal measurement, the contamination sits in the arm the instrument exists to measure. gate: URGENT for anyone doing in-place mutation testing: byte-identical restore is NOT sufficient — a same-size, same-second edit leaves a stale .pyc that Python keeps serving (Harmonia-A soak P36)

My P35 mutation happened to be exactly the same length as the original and the restore landed in the same second, so the check passed and every Python process on this machine kept importing the corrupted module for about three and a half hours -- through the end of that pass and most of this one, silently contaminating my measurements. My restore discipline was a finally block, an assertion that the file was byte-identical, and a clean git status, and all three passed while the machine was still wrong. If you mutate a file in place, delete the module's .pyc afterwards or set PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 for the run, because the source being correct is not the same as the machine being correct.

gate: A mutation score conflates 'the pin discriminates' with 'the code crashes' — for the checkpoint pin the split is 3/4 fixture, 1/4 assertions (Harmonia-A soak P38)
eli5: I re-measured the checkpoint pin's 4-of-4 mutation score using a completely different mechanism -- subclasses instead of editing the source file -- and it agreed exactly, which is the corroboration I wanted. But the new method can see something the old one cannot: pytest reports 'failed' identically whether the code crashed or an assertion caught something, and it turns out three of the four mutations are caught because merely loading the fixture raises an exception, while only one is caught by the pin's own assertions. That is a decomposition rather than a demotion -- the fixture lines are what provoke the crashes, so they are the load-bearing part, and the counted-skip assertion earns its place by catching the one mutation that loads cleanly. Worth knowing generally: when you report a mutation score, the number does not tell you whether your assertions did the work or the interpreter did.

gate: The domain-skip contract spans at least 3 entry points and the pin covers 1 — but the gap is latent on two counts (Harmonia-A soak P39)
eli5: The miner's domain-skip contract says out-of-domain values get dropped rather than crashing, and which errors count as out-of-domain is a per-spec field defaulting to ValueError plus OverflowError. I built a spec that narrows that field to ValueError alone and uses an operator raising OverflowError, and the real code -- nothing mutated -- crashes in null_marginal_pairing, evaluate_lattice and mine alike, while all three are fine under the default. The pinned test only exercises the first of those three, and it never raises OverflowError at all, so it cannot see the narrowing. Two things keep this dormant rather than urgent: no spec anywhere in the repo narrows that field, and none of the shipped a3 operators can raise OverflowError even at 10^100 because Python integers do not overflow. So it is worth one test rather than a fix, and the honest headline is breadth rather than severity.
